title: Fabric data agent creation - Microsoft Fabric | Microsoft Learn
summary: Microsoft Learn's conceptual reference for the Fabric data agent: a generally-available, configurable conversational Q&A artifact that lets users ask plain-language questions over governed Fabric data and get structured answers back. It walks through the question-to-query pipeline, the governance/precedence model that constrains agent behavior, how it differs from Fabric Copilot, and a list of current limitations.
audience: Architects and data platform leads evaluating whether to expose Fabric data as a conversational interface, and builders configuring a data agent's sources, instructions, and example queries.
why_it_matters: Data agents are the piece that turns a governed lakehouse/warehouse/semantic-model estate into something business users can query in natural language without writing SQL/DAX/KQL, but they inherit Purview governance and have firm scope/output limits that change how they should be designed into a multi-agent or Copilot-integrated architecture.
takeaways: A data agent acts as a read-only conversational router that picks the right data source and tool (NL2SQL, NL2DAX, NL2KQL, or Graph) per question, rather than being a single text-to-SQL engine.
Governance is layered with strict precedence: organizational policy beats workspace/role settings, which beat developer instructions, which beat end-user prompts.
Permissions for Power BI sources are looser than expected: Read access on the semantic model is enough for the agent to query it, Build is not required, though RLS/CLS still apply.
Output is intentionally constrained (5 sources max, 25x25 result cap, no write operations, no unstructured files) which matters when scoping what a data agent can realistically replace.
ALM tooling (Git integration, deployment pipelines, diagnostics) treats agent configuration as a promotable artifact, similar to other Fabric items.

claims.text: Within multi-agent application architectures on Fabric, a data agent functions as the conversational analytics component, connecting to governed OneLake data through lakehouses, warehouses, semantic models, and KQL databases.
A single data agent can combine up to five data sources in any mix of lakehouses, warehouses, KQL databases, Power BI semantic models, ontologies, and Microsoft Graph.

After identifying the relevant data source, the agent routes the question to a source-specific generator: NL2SQL for lakehouse/warehouse, NL2DAX for Power BI semantic models, NL2KQL for KQL databases, or a Microsoft Graph query for organizational data.
The agent enforces read-only, least-privilege access by executing under the requesting user's own credentials and permissions, so each query only reaches data that user is already authorized to view.

For Power BI semantic model sources, only Read permission on the model is required for the agent to retrieve schema and run queries; Build permission is not needed, though Row-Level and Column-Level Security still apply.

Agent behavior is governed by a four-layer precedence model, from highest to lowest: tenant-wide organizational policy, workspace/role-based governance settings, developer-supplied instructions and example queries, and finally end-user prompts; higher layers always override lower ones.

Purview Data Loss Prevention and access-restriction policies apply directly to data agent queries, and can block a query from running or strip sensitive results from an agent's response even when the agent is technically permitted to read the source.

Eventhouse KQL databases are queried in place by the agent with no data movement, and NL2KQL can use existing KQL user-defined functions; configurators are advised to scope to the most relevant tables and encourage time filters to keep responses fast over high-volume event data.

A data agent is a standalone, highly configurable artifact that can query across OneLake and semantic models and be invoked by external orchestrators, which distinguishes it from Fabric Copilots that are preconfigured, non-customizable, and scoped to in-product tasks like generating notebook or warehouse code.

Data agent configurations support application lifecycle management through built-in diagnostics, Git integration for version-controlling instructions and example queries, and deployment pipelines for promoting an agent from development to production workspaces.

Agent responses are capped at a maximum of 25 rows and 25 columns, and because prior chat turns can influence later answers, a request like asking for all rows for a year will still be limited to 25 rows even in follow-up questions within the same session.

A data agent cannot execute queries when its workspace capacity and its data source's workspace capacity are in different regions, so a lakehouse in one region paired with a data agent capacity in another region will fail.

The agent only ever generates read queries (SQL, DAX, or KQL) and never create, update, or delete statements, and it cannot directly query unstructured files such as PDF, DOCX, or TXT, or standalone lakehouse files unless those files are first ingested or exposed as tables.
